sections.h2: What should a seller know about Piscataway before listing?
sections.html:
Piscataway will not let a home change occupants without a Municipal Certificate of Continued Compliance. The requirement has applied to sales and rentals since January 1, 2019, and it is the step that most often sets the calendar for a closing.

The township sits on the south side of the Raritan Valley in Middlesex County, covering 18.79 square miles of land. Settlers from New England received land here in 1666, making Piscataway the fifth-oldest municipality in New Jersey, and it was incorporated in 1798. Today the Census Bureau counts 62,253 residents as of July 1, 2025, up 2.4 percent from the 2020 base.

Rutgers University defines much of the place. The Busch and Livingston campuses lie inside the township, along with SHI Stadium. Neighborhood names residents use include Arbor, Bound Brook Heights, Fellowship Farm, Johnson Park, Lake Nelson, New Market, North Stelton, Randolphville, Riverview Manor and Society Hill. Camp Kilmer, opened in 1941 on land in Piscataway and Edison, processed more than 2.5 million soldiers during World War II before closing in 2009.

sections.h2: How does the Piscataway MCCC inspection work?
sections.html:
The Community Development Department inspects each dwelling for fitness for habitation and issues the certificate if it passes. Inspections take place weekdays from 8 a.m. to noon and 1:30 to 3:30 p.m., excluding holidays, and inspectors show a township vehicle and photo identification at the door.

The township asks sellers to apply at least four weeks before closing. Applications and fees go to the MCCC office at the Public Works Center, reachable at (732) 562-2393 or mccc@piscatawaynj.org. Section 14-4 of the municipal code governs the program.

  • Single-family home, condo or townhome: $150 per unit.
  • Two-family: $150 per unit, so $300 in total.
  • Temporary MCCC: $125 per unit, available after an application is filed.
  • Reinspections: $100 per unit starting with the third inspection.

One rule catches many sellers: if work was done without a required permit, the permit must be obtained and any open permits closed before the certificate is issued. Dig out old deck, basement and kitchen permits early.

sections.h2: Why does Piscataway sell differently from nearby towns?
sections.html:
Its buyers are drawn by the university, a corporate base and highway access. The township lists companies such as Colgate-Palmolive's research and development operation, Hapag-Lloyd America, IEEE, GenScript Biotech, Cintas and a Pepsi bottling plant among its corporate residents.

  • Interstate 287 crosses the township with exits 6 through 9, and Route 18 reaches it along Hoes Lane.
  • The New Jersey Turnpike is close at East Brunswick Exit 9 and Edison Exit 10.
  • No train station stands inside Piscataway, but the Raritan Valley Line stops at Dunellen and the Northeast Corridor at Edison.
  • NJ Transit bus 114 serves Port Authority in Manhattan, and routes 65 and 66 go to Newark.

The school district runs eleven schools and enrolled 7,331 students in 2024 to 2025, including Piscataway High School. The district also includes three middle schools named Conackamack, Quibbletown and Schor.

sections.h2: What do Census figures show for Piscataway homes?
sections.html:
Values in Piscataway sit well above the national figure of $332,700. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates give a median owner-occupied value of $449,900, a median gross rent of $2,024 and median household income of $127,832.

Owners live in 63.8 percent of homes, and the township has 17,664 households averaging 2.95 people. About 48.9 percent of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher. Foreign-born residents make up 33.9 percent of the population, 30.7 percent identify as Asian alone, and 43.4 percent of those five and older speak another language at home.

sections.h2: How can I prepare a Piscataway house for the MCCC?
sections.html:
Preparation starts with paperwork, because the township treats unpermitted work as a hold on the certificate. The partial checklist on the township site is described as a guide to what homes most commonly fail, and it does not cover every possible reason for failure.

  • Submit the application and fee at least four weeks before the closing date.
  • Collect permits for decks, finished basements, additions, water heaters and electrical work, and close any that are still open.
  • Plan the visit for a weekday window, and expect inspectors to show photo identification.
  • Budget for the third inspection onward, which costs $100 per unit.
  • Ask whether a temporary certificate fits your timeline if repairs will run past closing.

Older housing stock is part of the picture. The Road Up Raritan Historic District holds nine historic homes along River Road and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1999, and a house dating to 1741 operates as a county museum. Owners in or near historic areas should ask the Planning Division what local review applies before promising a buyer exterior changes.

sections.h2: How do Piscataway taxes work for a seller?
sections.html:
Ask the township Tax Collector for a current statement before you set a closing date, because balances and installments change through the year. The tax office also publishes the township's rates.

In April 2026 the township announced a budget that lowered the municipal tax rate by another 4.72 percent to offset gains in property value. A lower rate does not guarantee a lower bill, since assessed values and county and school levies move too, so compare your own bill line by line.

Taxes and sewer charges can be paid online through the township website, which helps when a title company needs proof that accounts are current.

sections.h2: Who records the deed for a Piscataway sale?
sections.html:
The Middlesex County Clerk's registry in New Brunswick records deeds for Piscataway properties. The office opens weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4:10 p.m. and asks walk-in filers to arrive by 4 p.m.; appointments are optional but get priority.

A deed must say "Prepared by" and name the drafter, show the tax block, lot and consideration, and give a record-and-return address. Signatures must be original with the names printed beneath. A re-recorded deed needs a new affidavit, a new seller's residency form and a new cover sheet. Title companies commonly file electronically through the New Jersey County Recording system instead.

State forms go with the deed. Married sellers who file a joint state return may sign one Gross Income Tax form, while unmarried co-owners each sign their own, matched to their ownership share. A nonresident seller prepays at least 2 percent of the sale price. Heirs selling an inherited house sign according to their own residency.

sections.h2: Is a cash sale worth considering in Piscataway?
sections.html:
It can be, when a house is likely to fail the MCCC inspection, has open permits or has sat vacant. A cash buyer may accept the property without the repairs a seller would otherwise fund, but the certificate still comes before any change of occupancy, and the township also offers a temporary version at $125 per unit once an application is filed.

Ask any buyer who files the MCCC application, who pays the fees, and what happens if reinspections run past the second visit. Weigh the offer against what you would net after repairs, the seller's transfer fee and the months a listing may take.

faqs.q: Does Piscataway require an inspection to sell a house?
faqs.a: Yes. A Municipal Certificate of Continued Compliance is required when selling or renting a home, and the township asks for the application four weeks before closing.

faqs.q: How much does a Piscataway MCCC cost?
faqs.a: It costs $150 per unit for a single-family home, condo or townhome, $300 for a two-family, and $125 per unit for a temporary certificate. Reinspections cost $100 per unit starting with the third.

faqs.q: What happens if I did work in Piscataway without a permit?
faqs.a: The permit must be obtained and any open permits closed before the certificate is issued. Start that step early because it can hold up a closing.

faqs.q: Where is the Piscataway MCCC office?
faqs.a: It operates from the Public Works Center. Call (732) 562-2393 or email mccc@piscatawaynj.org for an appointment.
At the Middlesex County Clerk's registry at 75 Bayard Street in New Brunswick, or electronically through the county's e-recording service for title companies.
